title: In two planted tree cohorts, mass weighting reversed its effect on the southward response to warming
abstract: We tested whether living stem mass and surviving tree numbers gave the same geographic composition response to warming. We used the 2012 and 2013 cohorts from a two-site Minnesota experiment with six blocks, three warming levels and two rain levels. The geographic index was the negative species range-centre latitude, not a thermal index in C. With the same eight species, +3.1 C and ambient rain shifted survivor composition south in both cohorts. Mass weighting added 1.73 degrees latitude to this shift in the 2012 cohort but subtracted 1.59 degrees in the 2013 cohort. The paired difference was -3.32 degrees, with a site-adjusted block t interval of -4.22 to -2.42 and a Holm-adjusted p value of 0.0021 across four treatment tests. Both sites had this sign change. An exact observed partition separates species presence, surviving-number weighting and mass weighting without assigning size to absent survivors. But the 2013 cohort already had a northward size imbalance at its first census. Subtracting that diagnostic imbalance removed its negative biomass-response point estimate. The result shows that mass and survivor composition need not measure the same response after species arrival. It does not identify a causal cohort or growth effect, a thermal tracking fraction, or the share of the field response gap due to mortality. Small block numbers, the geographic proxy, first-season size differences, selected juvenile species and shared plots limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, figures, source hashes and retrieval instructions are included.
